_comment: M60-01 snapshot column policy. One entry per column of every covered table,
and for any column whose name says it carries an identity.
Treatments: keep | drop_column | drop_table | keep_gated | replace (text) | rekey_pseud (uuid, 11.16.3) | rekey_account (uuid, 11.16.3b).
A pass means a decision EXISTS, not that it is right. The gate cannot see
whether anyone thought about an entry, which is what reviewed_by is for.
Treatments: replace | drop_column | drop_table | keep | keep_gated

accounts.age_state.why: Operational or content metadata; carries no personal data.

accounts.created_at.why: 11.16.5: a shared month offset is a LINKABLE IDENTIFIER. Two dumps shifted by the same amount join row-for-row on every timestamp, so each snapshot uses its own offset, applied inside the snapshot and never recorded. This column is an EVENT time -- when a row came into existence or changed -- so shifting it preserves every interval and ordering the dataset exists to answer while denying cross-snapshot row alignment. Treated as `keep` this column is what makes two monthly dumps joinable.

accounts.deleted_at.why: Relative time is the research value. Absolute time is not an identifier (11.16.5).

accounts.email.why: The primary identifier. Replaced with a stable non-reversible placeholder: deterministic, so two rows with the same address still collide and a researcher can count distinct accounts, and irreversible because md5 of a known address is trivially reversed by brute force over the address space.

accounts.email_verified_at.why: A timestamp adjacent to the email column, not an identifier. Dropped rather than redacted: a null 'verified at' alongside a redacted email is the honest value, and a constant string here would read as 'verified'.

accounts.id.why: The account key every account_id foreign key points at. Re-keyed, not kept: a kept id is the value the re-keyed foreign keys must resolve TO, and leaving it raw is what makes a snapshot 'one column obscured'.

age_assessments.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the failure the requirement is 'most likely to be implemented backwards': rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous. The snapshot LOOKS de-identified and is not.

reader_body_copies.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the second join key the re-keying exists to preserve. The copy is a reader's OWN artefact, so preserving the join is what lets a researcher see that one account made one request, and re-keying is what stops that account being identified.

retention_body_requests.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the second join key the re-keying exists to preserve. The whole point of the row is WHICH reader asked and at what trust level, so the column has to survive as a join; trust_at_request is what makes the row meaningful and it is not an identity.

retention_proposal_votes.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the second join key the re-keying exists to preserve. A ballot is already unstackable per account, so re-keying preserves the one-vote-per-account property without naming the voter -- which is the privacy property retention_proposals.rs exists to hold.

works.redistribution.why: An AUTHOR'S OWN ASSERTION that this work may be redistributed (M45-14). Carried verbatim it tells a recipient which works are asserted-redistributable and which are not -- a fact about a real person's legal position, asserted for THIS instance's audience. drop_column, not keep_gated, and not redact, for the reason works.body_audience already carries in this file: absence is the only honest value. A gated copy still says the work is restricted; a constant says it less precisely. Dropping it removes the fact. The snapshot is a research corpus, not a record of who asserted what.

reader_body_copies.plain_text.why: The reader-visible body, in its two renderings. Treated as ONE decision with chapter_revisions.plain_text and .sanitized_html: masking the text alone would republish the whole body as HTML, which is the note those two entries already carry. Gated on 11.16.6's condition -- a snapshot taken while the instance is in `cache` may carry bodies, one taken in `aggregate` may not. The privacy point beyond the chapter case: this copy belongs to ONE reader, so account_id is re-keyed separately and the dump cannot say whose copy it is. Surfaced by the CONTENT_NAME_RE fan-out added in this commit, which exists precisely because the gate was silent on it.

reader_body_copies.sanitized_html.why: The reader-visible body, in its two renderings. Treated as ONE decision with chapter_revisions.plain_text and .sanitized_html: masking the text alone would republish the whole body as HTML, which is the note those two entries already carry.

works_index.body_text.why: The full text of EVERY work on the instance, in one NOT NULL column. drop_table, not keep_gated, and the reason is the shape: the gate would be evaluated once, for the table, so a snapshot taken in the wrong mode publishes every body at once rather than refusing one. works_index is the search index and exists only to serve search, which is rebuilt from chapter_revisions -- gated per mode and re-derivable by a recipient. Dropping it loses nothing a research corpus needs.

roadmap_suggestions.raw_text.why: A reader's OWN submitted prose, freely written, NOT NULL. Not body text in 11.16's sense: it is not a work's text, it is a person's. No mode-based gate is right here, because a `cache` instance would publish every suggestion ever made. The suggestion's existence, its card association and its ballot history all survive; the prose does not.

critique_queue.excerpt.why: An excerpt of a FORUM POST -- a person's words, not a work's text, for the same reason as roadmap_suggestions.raw_text. The queue's research value is which posts were queued and in what order, and posted_at plus position give exactly that without the prose.

tasting_samples.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. Same reasoning and same treatment as arena_weights.account_id and arena_ballots.account_id; 11.16.3b. Using rekey_text here would emit a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous -- the snapshot would LOOK de-identified and would not be.

tasting_responses.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. Same reasoning and same treatment as arena_weights.account_id and arena_ballots.account_id; 11.16.3b. Using rekey_text here would emit a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous -- the snapshot would LOOK de-identified and would not be.

tasting_responses.session_id.why: Not a foreign key and not an identity: an opaque per-calibration-session label this instance minted, so it identifies nobody outside the snapshot and no row can be joined to an account through it. §49.5 bounds a session's sample count, which is the only thing it is used for, and dropping it would make the per-session bound unverifiable from a snapshot. keep_gated rather than keep: a session id is low-risk on its own but is a join key, so it is exported only with the de-identified dataset and not with the smaller ones.

work_tags.confirmation.why: An enum the author or a reader applied to a tag, with no identity in it: 'unconfirmed', 'reader', 'wrangler' or 'inaccurate'. It records WHO confirmed in the coarse sense of which class of actor, and never WHICH one -- flagged_by holds the identity, and that is the column that needs re-keying, not this. Keeping it is what makes §49.2 auditable in a snapshot: without it, a de-identified dataset cannot distinguish a counted tag from an uncounted one and the gravity contribution cannot be reproduced.

work_tags.flagged_by.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. Same reasoning and same treatment as arena_weights.account_id and arena_ballots.account_id; 11.16.3b. Using rekey_text here would emit a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous -- the snapshot would LOOK de-identified and would not be. Here it is the ONLY column naming who flagged a tag, so leaving it as a bare UUID would put a real account id into a published dataset while every neighbouring column read as pseudonymous.

work_tags.flagged_at.why: When a tag was flagged. Timestamps are offset on the instance-wide shift so relative order survives and the absolute instant does not, matching every other created_at/updated_at in the policy. §49.2's value is in the ordering -- an inaccurate flag's effect has to be visible as preceding later re-confirmations -- which an offset preserves.

tasting_samples.sample_offset.why: A character offset into the work's text, so the 300-word window §49.5 shows can be reproduced. It is a position in a public document, not a fact about a person, and the offset is what stops the sample from being unreproducible. Dropping it would make every sampling decision in the published dataset unverifiable.

tasting_responses.uncertainty_at_draw.why: The confidence the active-learning selector had in its own pick, recorded at draw time so §49.5's 'picked by uncertainty' is a checkable claim rather than an assertion. No identity in it, and it is exactly the number an offline evaluation of the selector needs.

tasting_responses.verdict.why: 'like' or 'dislike'. The signal itself; §49.5 requires it non-null.

tasting_responses.reason.why: The required reason tag. §49.5 makes the reason the labelled signal, so a snapshot without it cannot train or audit anything.

tasting_responses.free_text.why: The reader's own free-text 'not for me: ___'. Free text is the one column in this migration where a person may have written anything at all, including their own name or someone else's, and it is the only one no reviewer can screen in advance. §49.5 keeps the reason TAGS as the signal precisely because free text is not reviewable, so dropping this loses nothing the mechanism relies on. The enumerated reason survives; the sentence a reader typed does not.

tasting_samples.id.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

tasting_responses.id.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

tasting_responses.sample_id.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

tasting_samples.work_id.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

tasting_samples.created_at.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

tasting_responses.created_at.why: Migration 0099 primary/foreign key or creation timestamp, with no personal data in it; matches the treatment every other id and created_at column carries.

taste_signals.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the failure the requirement is 'most likely to be implemented backwards': rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural test still passes. taste_signals.account_id in particular is the join that makes 49.6's import analysable at all -- per-account weights are meaningless once you cannot tell whose they are -- so breaking it silently turns the import into unattributable aggregate.

taste_signal_imports.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the failure the requirement is 'most likely to be implemented backwards': rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural test still passes. taste_signals.account_id in particular is the join that makes 49.6's import analysable at all -- per-account weights are meaningless once you cannot tell whose they are -- so breaking it silently turns the import into unattributable aggregate. taste_signal_imports.account_id additionally anchors the import's provenance to the reader who asked for it, so the re-key must be identical across both tables or the import cannot be traced to a snapshot account.

work_highlights.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b, and this is the failure the requirement is 'most likely to be implemented backwards': rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash, which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural test still passes. 50.1 needs the join for a specific reason: a highlight counts ONCE toward a work's gravity, and 'once' is per READER. Break this key and the distinct-reader count becomes a highlight count, which is exactly the influence purchase 33.2 forbids -- with nothing failing.

works.generated_content_posture.why: Three-valued instance policy, no personal data. 'forbid' | 'disclose' | 'allow' describes how the INSTANCE handles generated content, and the value is a property of the work's publication, not of anybody who wrote it -- which is why it can be kept even though works.title beside it is gated. Keeping it is also what makes a snapshot auditable: a reviewer reading a dataset has to be able to see which works were disclosed, because that changes how a downstream use of the text should be interpreted. Replacing or dropping it would leave a disclosed work indistinguishable from an allowed one, which is the specific thing §51.1's 'allow accepts and does not label' creates.

works.generated_declared_at.why: When the author made their own declaration, and it is the only column of the pair that is about a person rather than about the work. The posture already says whether the work was declared generated under 'disclose' and 'allow', so the dataset keeps the fact and drops the timestamp -- and the timestamp is the part that carries identity: it is a moment a named author asserted something about their own writing. A snapshot's purpose is aggregate retention (11.16.6), and 'this work is disclosed as generated' is the only part of it an aggregate reader needs. Dropping the column rather than replacing it is deliberate: a bucket or shift of a timestamp invents precision that a re-identification attempt does not need but a reader of the dataset would assume is real.

concierge_sessions.id.why: The session's own surrogate key. Carries no identity of its own: it is referenced by nothing outside this table and names no person. `keep` rather than `drop_column` because the table's primary key is the only way a row is addressed, and a snapshot that drops it cannot answer 'was this the same render' -- which is the question a reader's own history exists to answer.

concierge_sessions.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b: rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous -- the snapshot LOOKS de-identified and is not. This table stores what ONE READER was shown, so dropping or replacing the account would not merely obscure it: it would leave rows that belong to no one and cannot be joined to the reading history that explains them.

concierge_sessions.mood.why: A §15.8 mood key the reader typed. It is an expression of preference, which is behavioural data about a person -- so this is kept deliberately and is exactly why account_id must be re-keyed rather than dropped: a free-text preference with no owner is harmless, and one attached to a stable id is not. Not replaced: a constant would make every row's mood identical and destroy the column's only value.

concierge_sessions.budget_minutes.why: Minutes the reader stated they had. Operational metadata, no identity. It is a small integer and so quasi-identifying on its own (a budget of 5 minutes is rare), which is an argument for keeping the ACCOUNT re-keyed rather than for changing this column -- the re-key already removes the join to a person, and perturbing the value would destroy the budget/cut relationship §54.4 exists to expose.

concierge_sessions.work_ids.why: A JSON array of the work ids the queue returned, in order. The whole research value of this table is the ORDER -- it is a rendering, not a set -- so it is kept verbatim. Work ids are not user ids and carry no identity; the risk this column carries is that it plus a stable account_id would reconstruct one reader's taste profile, which is why the re-key on account_id is the decision that matters here.

concierge_sessions.estimated_minutes.why: A derived duration total. Arithmetic on word counts; no identity, no free text. `keep` because it is the column that makes a budget cut legible after the fact, and dropping it would leave a truncated queue that cannot be checked against the work ids beside it.

concierge_sessions.truncated_at.why: An integer index or NULL. No identity. Kept because NULL-vs-0 is a distinction the schema exists to hold ('nothing was cut' is not 'cut at index 0'), and collapsing either to a default would make the table assert something false about §54.4's behaviour.

concierge_sessions.rate_source.why: Either 'observed' or 'default', CHECK-constrained to those two. No identity. Kept because it distinguishes a queue cut on the reader's own reading speed from one cut on the instance default, which is a difference in how the number was produced rather than in the number.

concierge_sessions.created_at.why: 11.16.5: a shared month offset is a LINKABLE IDENTIFIER, so each snapshot uses its own offset, applied inside the snapshot and never recorded. This is an EVENT time -- when the row came into existence -- so shifting it preserves every interval and ordering the dataset exists to answer while denying cross-snapshot row alignment. On concierge_sessions it is load-bearing for a second reason: a session is only interpretable against the moment it was rendered, and a reader's queue changes with the catalogue, so an unshifted timestamp would silently attribute one month's queue to another.

wip_watches.id.why: The watch's own surrogate key. Names no person and is referenced by nothing outside this table. `keep` because `mark_watched` addresses a watch by id and a snapshot that dropped it could not answer whether a notification had already been sent -- the one fact §54.5's UNIQUE exists to guarantee.

wip_watches.account_id.why: A UUID foreign key to accounts.id, so it must be re-keyed with snapshot_account -- the SAME derivation accounts.id uses, on the account salt, so the join survives. 11.16.3b: rekey_text emits a `snp_` TEXT hash which cannot be compared with a uuid, so the relationship to accounts is destroyed while every behavioural column still reads as pseudonymous -- the snapshot LOOKS de-identified and is not. This table stores what ONE READER was shown, so dropping or replacing the account would not merely obscure it: it would leave rows that belong to no one and cannot be joined to the reading history that explains them. Here it is sharper still: (account_id, work_id) is the UNIQUE key, so a snapshot that replaced this column with a constant would collapse every watch in the dump into one row and destroy the one-notification-per-watch property the constraint exists to enforce.

wip_watches.work_id.why: A UUID foreign key to works.id, kept verbatim so a snapshot can join watches to the works being watched. Works are public content and carry no identity. NOT re-keyed: rekey_account would break the join to works, and there is nothing to protect here that works.id does not already expose.

wip_watches.notified_at.why: The moment the notification was written, or NULL while pending. Shifted per snapshot as an event time. NULL must be preserved rather than defaulted: 'nobody has been told yet' and 'told at some invented time' are different facts about §54.5, and only the first is true of this column.

wip_watches.created_at.why: 11.16.5 as above: event time, shifted per snapshot so two dumps do not join row-for-row on the fact that a reader opened two WIP works in the same hour. Here it is also the ONLY ordering column, so the offset must preserve ordering -- which shifting does and dropping would not.
